cards.title: Measure Shopify conversion and RPV with corrected revenue and sessions
cards.summary: Build store reporting from net sales plus shipping and preferably GA4 sessions, while checking individual metrics against profitability to prevent optimization artifacts.
cards.use_when: Creating a Shopify conversion dashboard or evaluating whether a page, offer, or traffic change improved ecommerce performance.

cards.title: Use split tests for big swings and adequate scale, not endless micro-tweaks
cards.summary: Implement obvious high-leverage fixes directly, reserve controlled experiments for consequential hypotheses, and evaluate them with revenue-quality metrics.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch an A/B test on a PDP or whether to implement a clear conversion improvement without testing.

cards.title: Configure checkout and shipping as deliberate economic levers
cards.summary: Keep checkout friction low, use shipping as a tested margin and AOV lever, and avoid treating free shipping as an automatic conversion requirement.
cards.use_when: Configuring checkout, setting shipping charges, or choosing a free-shipping threshold for an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Build landing pages as a stacked purchase argument
cards.summary: Sequence a landing page from immediate clarity through education, offer, proof and risk reversal so each section resolves the next purchase question.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing a cold-traffic product landing page, advertorial, or PDP that must convert a shopper to a first purchase.

cards.title: Create message-matched landing pages for each ad angle
cards.summary: A specific acquisition angle needs a page that continues its promise, proof and language instead of burying that benefit among many others.
cards.use_when: Running cold acquisition campaigns with different customer personas, problem states, creative concepts, or offers.

cards.title: Turn feature-heavy copy into benefit, mechanism, and differentiated proof
cards.summary: Lead copy with the buyer's desired outcome, explain how the product produces it, and use review research to find credible differentiators.
cards.use_when: Rewriting a PDP or landing page whose hero and sections read like product specifications rather than reasons to purchase.

cards.title: Prioritize CRO work with ICE and mobile behavior evidence
cards.summary: Score candidate changes by impact, confidence, and ease, then use mobile heatmaps and recordings to continuously refill the backlog.
cards.use_when: Choosing which PDP, landing-page, cart, or checkout changes to implement first when the store has many possible CRO ideas.

cards.title: Build claim-matched proof, then close with risk reversal
cards.summary: Feature visual reviews and testimonials that prove the active purchase claim, then resolve residual purchase risk with a clear guarantee or returns promise.
cards.use_when: Selecting reviews, testimonials, before-and-afters, and guarantee language for a PDP or conversion landing page.

cards.title: Audit checkout abandonment by friction category, not by one headline rate
cards.summary: Use known abandonment causes to inspect surprise costs, delivery, trust, account creation, form length, returns, and recovery flows.
cards.use_when: Auditing cart and checkout performance or deciding which checkout friction should be fixed before redesigning the entire flow.

cards.title: Test checkout extras and price presentation without hiding the true total
cards.summary: Manage shipping, tax, and fee presentation so shoppers understand the full cost before committing, while testing economics against revenue and margin.
cards.use_when: Setting shipping charges, free-shipping thresholds, tax presentation, or subscription pricing display on product pages, cart, and checkout.

cards.title: Design checkout for guest purchase, express pay, and minimal form effort
cards.summary: A checkout should make buying as fast as possible through guest access, wallet payments, concise forms, transparent cost, and visible returns terms.
cards.use_when: Configuring Shopify or another ecommerce checkout, or deciding whether a one-page versus multi-step checkout test is worth running.

cards.title: Treat returns policy as a conversion and profitability trade-off
cards.summary: A visible, understandable returns policy can reduce hesitation, but overly generous free returns can increase return behavior and operational cost.
cards.use_when: Deciding how prominently to feature returns, whether to offer free returns, or how to evaluate a more generous policy in fashion or other return-prone categories.

cards.title: Only run A/B tests that can reach valid decisions
cards.summary: Assess sample needs, contamination, multi-click exposure, and time-to-purchase before treating an A/B result as evidence.
cards.use_when: Planning a landing-page, PDP, checkout, or offer test—or evaluating a claimed CRO winner from an agency or internal team.

cards.title: Use revenue and contribution per visitor to judge CRO quality
cards.summary: Conversion rate is useful but heavily shaped by traffic mix, so evaluate page changes using revenue or contribution generated per visitor as well.
cards.use_when: Choosing CRO program KPIs, comparing acquisition traffic quality, or judging whether a conversion improvement helped the store financially.

cards.title: Reject conversion wins that damage repeat purchase and lifetime value
cards.summary: Aggressive claims or dark patterns can improve front-end conversion while increasing returns, chargebacks, and long-term customer-value loss.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a high-performing acquisition claim, landing-page angle, subscription tactic, or checkout persuasion method before scaling it.

cards.title: Raise order value with positioned bundles, thresholds, and post-purchase upsells
cards.summary: Use a problem-solving routine, shipping or gift thresholds, and relevant one-click upsells to grow order value without relying on blanket discounts.
cards.use_when: Improving AOV and revenue per visitor for a product that already converts individually, especially on landing pages, cart drawers, and post-purchase flows.

cards.title: Send unaware cold traffic to a story-led conversion page
cards.summary: VSLs, advertorials, listicles, and quizzes need a dedicated page that develops the problem and mechanism before asking an unfamiliar shopper to buy.
cards.use_when: Choosing a destination for cold, problem-aware, or unaware acquisition creative that cannot rely on existing brand familiarity.

cards.title: Baseline product-research checklist before any tool
cards.summary: Four pass/fail criteria — margin, problem solved, existing content, shipping weight — that any dropshipping product must clear before deeper research.
cards.use_when: Screening a candidate product or deciding whether a product found via ad spy, Instagram or TikTok is worth further analysis.

cards.title: Three fastest ways to fail at product selection
cards.summary: The source's three anti-patterns to avoid: selling what you personally like, copying a competitor as a beginner, and choosing a product with no content online.
cards.use_when: Stress-testing a product idea before committing budget, or diagnosing why previous tests failed.

cards.title: Random, un-niched products as the beginner entry path
cards.summary: For first-time dropshippers the source recommends deliberately random utility products outside mainstream niches to sidestep competition and high ad costs.
cards.use_when: Choosing a first product or first test when you have little experience and no brand equity.

cards.title: Meta Ad Library method: find dropshippers via generic keywords
cards.summary: Free method that surfaces live dropshipping ads by searching generic offer keywords and filtering to active ads — then cross-checking saturation.
cards.use_when: Starting product research with no paid tools, or validating whether other stores are currently advertising a product.

cards.title: TikTok cross-check for content supply and demand
cards.summary: Use TikTok to confirm there is usable creative for the product and treat TikTok saturation as acceptable as long as Facebook saturation is low.
cards.use_when: After a product passes the ad-library check, to confirm you have ad footage and to gauge relative saturation across platforms.

cards.title: Instagram Reels feed-training method for product discovery
cards.summary: Turn a fresh Instagram account's Reels feed into a stream of live dropshipping ads by seeding the algorithm with likes on physical-product videos.
cards.use_when: Daily passive product hunting, especially when you want product ideas to come to you rather than searching manually.

cards.title: Winning Hunter paid research: drop-ship filter and competitor thresholds
cards.summary: Use a paid ad-spy tool's dropship filter and AI competitor search to shortlist products, then apply explicit store-count thresholds before testing.
cards.use_when: When you want one tool to surface dropshipping ads and count competitors, and can afford a subscription.

cards.title: Daily research log and 3-to-1-to-1 selection funnel
cards.summary: Keep a Google Sheet of candidates with buy price, intended sell price and competitor notes, then narrow three products to one test per day.
cards.use_when: Setting up a repeatable daily product-research routine and deciding what to actually launch.

cards.title: Blue Ocean logic: saturated means demand, not dead
cards.summary: Saturation proves demand exists; the opportunity is to serve the same product to an audience nobody is targeting rather than to find a brand-new product.
cards.use_when: When your best-margin candidates all look crowded and you are tempted to abandon them or compete head-on.

cards.title: Geo-arbitrage: move proven US/UK products into untapped markets
cards.summary: Take a product already validated by US or UK advertising volume and run it in a market where it has not yet been shown.
cards.use_when: You have a proven product with strong English-language ad evidence and want lower competition than the source market.

cards.title: Angle pivoting: rebuild a saturated product around a new avatar
cards.summary: Keep the product, change the buyer: identify subsets of customers nobody is targeting and build the whole message around their specific situation.
cards.use_when: When a product is validated but competing ads all speak to one generic audience, and you need a differentiated campaign.

cards.title: Verify blue oceans by auditing what competitors are not doing
cards.summary: A two-step routine: find a problem-solving product, then audit competitor ads to locate the audience or angle none of them occupy.
cards.use_when: Systematically generating differentiated angles for any saturated product you are considering.

cards.title: Judging product quality: real value versus viral junk
cards.summary: Distinguish products that solve a durable human problem and hold margin from cheap trend items that rely on novelty and have no utility.
cards.use_when: Rejecting candidates during any research method, or deciding whether a trending item deserves a test.

cards.title: What a trained Instagram Reels feed yields and how to read it
cards.summary: Practical expectations for the Reels method: a mix of junk and winners, and a qualification step on AliExpress before logging a product.
cards.use_when: Running the Reels discovery loop and deciding which of the surfaced products to keep.

cards.title: Target Massive Stagnant Categories Instead of Educating Consumers
cards.summary: Pick huge existing commodity categories with a 'sea of sameness' so you skip consumer education and compete on differentiation rather than category creation.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product category to enter or reinvent, especially when deciding between a novel category and an established commodity.

cards.title: Force-Apply Outside Cultural Shifts to Create Creative Tension
cards.summary: Identify a macro cultural trend from a different domain and bolt it onto the stagnant category to produce an 'intersection of familiar and novel'.
cards.use_when: Developing the core concept or brand world for a commodity product that needs to feel culturally current rather than functionally new.

cards.title: The One Iteration Rule: Change Exactly One Product Variable
cards.summary: Limit reinvention to one major variable from the category's core expectation, because changing two or more makes the product too novel for adoption.
cards.use_when: Deciding how far to deviate from a familiar product format, scent, form, function or price point during concept design.

cards.title: Cross-Industry Aesthetic Theft to Force Differentiation
cards.summary: Borrow design architecture from a completely unrelated industry — the further apart the dots, the more powerful the differentiation.
cards.use_when: Generating packaging and brand-visual direction for a category where all incumbents share the same visual language.

cards.title: Naming Architecture from a Single Jumping-Off Word
cards.summary: Derive brand names from one emotional 'jumping-off word' tied to the product's ultimate goal, with the holy grail being one word and four letters.
cards.use_when: Running a brand naming process for a reinvented commodity product where the name must carry the new positioning.

cards.title: Iterate One Variable on a Proven Category
cards.summary: Enter large existing categories and change exactly one major variable to stay familiar-but-novel.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product or category to build in, or deciding how bold a repositioning should be

cards.title: Hunt for Cultural Shifts a Category Has Missed
cards.summary: The opportunity sits between a macro cultural shift and a stagnant category that hasn't absorbed it yet.
cards.use_when: Scanning a stuck or commoditized aisle for a repositioning opportunity

cards.title: Cross-Industry Theft to Create Creative Tension
cards.summary: Steal aesthetics and mechanics from far-away industries; the further apart the dots, the more powerful the idea.
cards.use_when: Generating distinct product, packaging or brand directions in a saturated category

cards.title: Design for the Familiar-Novel Intersection
cards.summary: Land products at the intersection of familiar and novel: too familiar loses differentiation, too novel kills trial.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether a concept is differentiated enough to matter yet easy enough to adopt

cards.title: Simplify Instead of Demonstrating Sophistication
cards.summary: Best entrepreneurs simplify complex ideas; over-complication is often ego and weakens the pitch.
cards.use_when: Tightening a pitch, product story, or positioning that sounds impressive but isn't landing

cards.title: Brand Naming Constraints: One Word, Four Letters
cards.summary: Start naming from a core feeling word tied to the product's goal, aiming for one word and four letters.
cards.use_when: Naming a new brand or product line

cards.title: Reimagine the Aisle as the Consumer's Experience
cards.summary: Walk the actual aisle and study shopper behavior to find the real pain the category ignores.
cards.use_when: Doing first-hand category research before defining a product concept

cards.title: Translate Benefits on Packaging, Not Features
cards.summary: Sell the outcome word ('sleep', 'beauty') instead of the ingredient name consumers can't decode.
cards.use_when: Writing product-page, packaging or shelf copy for a technical or unfamiliar product

cards.title: Look at What Everybody Else Does and Do the Opposite
cards.summary: A single structural contrast — like everyone is round, so we go square — can be the whole differentiator.
cards.use_when: Designing packaging or page layout in a visually homogeneous category

cards.title: Run Trend Trips with a 24-Hour Make Cycle
cards.summary: Kick off a trend trip with macro trends, assign in-field scavenger hunts, and turn findings into presented concepts within 24 hours.
cards.use_when: Planning a trend or inspiration trip intended to produce sellable concepts, not a photo library

cards.title: Pitch Buyers to Improve, Not to Prove
cards.summary: Bring concepts to retailers asking for feedback, not approval — especially for early product direction.
cards.use_when: Preparing to show a concept to retail buyers or partners

cards.title: Solve the Work in the Creative Before Research
cards.summary: Resolve concept direction by making it, then use qualitative feedback and retailer reaction to guide the choice.
cards.use_when: Choosing between two or three distinct concept directions

cards.title: Use 'If It's Hard, It's Probably Wrong' as a Signal
cards.summary: Treat friction and lack of flow as diagnostic signals, though genuine breakthroughs can require an uphill phase first.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep pushing a concept or change direction

cards.title: Build as an Artisan Operator
cards.summary: Combine creative imagination with predictable operating discipline — supply chain, finance, controls — rather than choosing one.
cards.use_when: Building the team, culture or operating model for a consumer brand

cards.title: Treat Selling as Transfer of Emotion and Energy
cards.summary: Early retail wins came from persistence and contagious belief, not from buyers believing in the product first.
cards.use_when: Selling into independent retailers, distributors or any gatekeeper as an unknown brand

cards.title: Time to Fun (TTF): the onboarding metric that predicts retention
cards.summary: Measure how long it takes a first-time user to reach a moment of genuine fun or value, and ruthlessly cut that time.
cards.use_when: Designing onboarding, first session, registration flow, or first-purchase experience for a product or store.

cards.title: Borrow low-TTF tactics from restaurants, samples and arrival rituals
cards.summary: Small, immediate sensory payoffs at the start of an experience lower perceived wait and raise engagement.
cards.use_when: Designing the first minutes of an in-person experience, or translating those mechanics to a digital first impression.

cards.title: White-space scan: look for a category with no brand anyone can name
cards.summary: Walk the aisles or the market looking for high-frequency purchase categories where customers cannot name a single brand — that absence is an opening.
cards.use_when: Sourcing new product or brand ideas in consumer categories.

cards.title: Sell the farm, not the chicken: origin story as differentiation
cards.summary: For commodity products, build the brand around the origin story and the life behind the product rather than the product specification.
cards.use_when: Differentiating a commodity or unbranded product where the physical product is hard to distinguish.

cards.title: Altruism plus narcissism: the two-sided consumer brand framework
cards.summary: A durable consumer brand delivers a self-interested benefit and a feel-good benefit at the same time.
cards.use_when: Positioning a new consumer brand or reframing an existing product's benefits.

cards.title: Jumping-off words: a repeatable naming method for brands
cards.summary: Start naming from a single word that captures what the brand must represent, then generate names from it.
cards.use_when: Naming a brand, product line or sub-brand and you need a starting constraint rather than a blank page.

cards.title: Change of presentation: reframe a rejection instead of accepting it
cards.summary: When a customer rejects a product, change how it is presented before concluding they don't like it.
cards.use_when: You see low trial, low repeat or flat engagement and are tempted to conclude the product or audience is wrong.

cards.title: Familiar plus novel: how to reposition a commodity format
cards.summary: Take a recognized product or format and add one clear element of novelty rather than inventing from scratch.
cards.use_when: Developing a new product in a crowded commodity category.

cards.title: When a hard business is the wrong business: recognize capital intensity
cards.summary: The source's rule of thumb is that if it's hard, it may be wrong — distinguish difficulty you can iterate out of from structural economics you can't.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep funding a venture, particularly retail, physical or capital-intensive consumer concepts.

cards.title: Incubator model: build the concept, hire a CEO, then step back
cards.summary: Create the idea, assemble the team and capital, then bring in an operator — and expect the handoff to be the hardest part.
cards.use_when: Founders who want to keep originating ideas without running the company long term.

cards.title: Inverse international expansion sequence to dodge US ad auction saturation
cards.summary: Enter secondary English-speaking markets in the order Australia, UK, Europe, Canada, then US to build dominant share before competitors saturate Meta auctions.
cards.use_when: Planning geographic expansion for an established ecommerce brand that has product-market fit in one market and is deciding which country to enter next.

cards.title: Why secondary English-speaking markets are cheaper to win first
cards.summary: Entering Australia, UK, Canada and Europe before the US exploits lower auction competition and English-language reuse while the US remains saturated.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to launch in a smaller English-speaking market first instead of the US, or comparing cost of entry across candidate countries.

cards.title: Product Selection Over Brand: The Fast Ecommerce Play
cards.summary: Prioritise finding a trending product in an under-served market over building a brand if your goal is fast ecommerce growth.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in brand building or rapid product acquisition for a new ecommerce venture.

cards.title: Inverse Geographic Market Entry Sequence
cards.summary: Enter secondary English-speaking markets before the US to secure first-mover advantage and avoid saturated Meta ad auctions.
cards.use_when: Planning international expansion for an ecommerce brand and deciding which market to enter first.

cards.title: Trend Spotting Through Deliberate Observation
cards.summary: Identify tipping trends by paying close attention to repeated signals and asking follow-up questions instead of dismissing them.
cards.use_when: Searching for a new product or market opportunity and needing a repeatable way to spot emerging trends.

cards.title: Using the Facebook Ads Library to Find Positioning Gaps
cards.summary: Scrape the Facebook ads library to find a trending product, map all its use cases, then target an unserved avatar with unique positioning.
cards.use_when: Sourcing products and developing unique positioning from existing market activity.

cards.title: Riding a Trend Wave to Build a Sustainable Business
cards.summary: Use a trending hero product to generate cash, then build brand and add evergreen secondary products before the trend declines.
cards.use_when: Managing a fast-growing ecommerce brand that depends on a trend-driven hero product.

cards.title: Competition and CPM Dynamics in Facebook Ad Auctions
cards.summary: Understand that Facebook is an auction where a second or third competitor for the same product grossly increases CPMs and changes the business.
cards.use_when: Assessing the long-term viability of a product niche or deciding when to pivot.

cards.title: Skill Gaps as the Constraint on Sustainable Growth
cards.summary: Identify and close the specific skill gaps that prevent your ecommerce business from scaling beyond its initial product success.
cards.use_when: A brand has achieved rapid product-led growth but is now plateauing or declining due to founder limitations.

cards.title: Hiring a Replacement CEO: Archetype and Retention
cards.summary: Define the exact archetype the business needs before hiring a replacement CEO, and trial candidates for six months if possible.
cards.use_when: Stepping back from the CEO role of an ecommerce brand you founded.

cards.title: Exposure Therapy for Founder Anxiety and Panic
cards.summary: Face anxiety-triggering opportunities deliberately rather than avoiding them, and give yourself permission to make mistakes.
cards.use_when: A founder is experiencing anxiety or panic attacks and is considering declining a significant opportunity because of them.

cards.title: Motivation Shift from External to Internal Drivers
cards.summary: Recognise when your drive shifts from proving others wrong to intrinsic purpose, and choose your peer group accordingly.
cards.use_when: Reflecting on what actually motivates you and managing competitive impulses as a founder.

cards.title: Ecommerce Exit Multiples and Timing
cards.summary: Understand the valuation ranges for different ecommerce business models and the importance of market timing when selling.
cards.use_when: Planning to sell an ecommerce brand or assessing what your business might be worth.

cards.title: Protecting Black Friday Trade After Logistics Failures
cards.summary: Do not let logistics and compliance failures cost you Black Friday, which the source says generates around 80% of his profits in two months.
cards.use_when: Managing ecommerce operations and third-party logistics ahead of peak trading periods.

cards.title: Retail-Distributed Brands Command Higher Exit Valuations
cards.summary: Target niche product categories with retail exposure to access higher exit valuations and more stable business economics.
cards.use_when: Choosing a product category or planning a brand that could attract acquisition interest.

cards.title: Building an AI-Era Service Arbitrage
cards.summary: Sell AI-enabled services to traditional businesses that do not understand the tools, creating an information arbitrage.
cards.use_when: A beginner wanting to reach a first $10,000 per month without building a full product business.

cards.title: When to Focus on the Main Business vs. Saving Side Projects
cards.summary: Resist diverting attention to failing side businesses when your main brand needs you; the source calls his diversion a stupid use of time.
cards.use_when: A founder is spreading attention across multiple businesses and one main brand is struggling.

cards.title: The Founder Trait Trap in Hiring and Business Design
cards.summary: Avoid hiring people who are the opposite of you, and avoid abandoning the traits that made the business successful.
cards.use_when: Hiring senior leaders or scaling an ecommerce business past founder-led operations.

cards.title: Brand as a Defensive Moat for Ecommerce
cards.summary: Build a brand layer on top of a trending product to survive competitors entering and the power law of competition.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to invest in brand building relative to aggressive acquisition.
